description: We are a team of passionate and curious innovators excited about space exploration, lunar science, and technology. Our goal is to develop Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a solution that helps identify and evaluate safe and suitable landing locations on the Moon using scientific data, satellite imagery, and innovative technologies.
summary: LUNAR is a prototype decision-support application designed to examine terrain and celestial visibility at a provisional lunar South Pole location. To address the challenge of lunar landing-site environment assessment, it combines NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data at multiple spatial resolutions with DE440-based SPICE ephemerides. Its terrain engine generates azimuth-dependent horizon profiles, while its visibility model estimates the apparent portions of the Sun and Earth disks visible over time. An interactive dashboard presents terrain skylines, celestial geometry, visibility timelines, observer-height sensitivity and sampled mission-window comparisons. The project helps make local environmental constraints, assumptions and data limitations inspectable rather than hiding them in a single site score. The current demonstration covers one provisional Site01 test point, a 45 km terrain range and a 48-hour interval. It does not predict DSN connectivity or electrical power.
details:
What LUNAR Does

LUNAR (Lunar Environment Intelligence and Mission Planning System) is a software-based decision-support prototype for examining terrain-obstructed sunlight and geometric Earth visibility at a provisional lunar South Pole location.

How It Works

The terrain workflow combines NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data: a 5 m/pixel local Site01 DEM and regional 80 m/pixel terrain data. A regional 20 m dataset was also used for cross-resolution consistency checks. The system builds an azimuth-dependent terrain horizon using 3,600 directions at 0.1-degree spacing, extending the sampled regional terrain horizon to 45 km.

The astronomical workflow uses NAIF SPICE and the DE440 planetary ephemeris to calculate apparent Sun and Earth directions in a lunar reference frame. These calculations are sampled every five minutes over a 48-hour interval. The application estimates the visible fraction of each apparent celestial disk against the sampled terrain skyline.

An interactive Streamlit dashboard presents terrain profiles, celestial geometry, visibility timelines, observer-height comparisons and sampled mission-delay windows.

Validation

Four SPICE timelines—Sun and Earth at observer heights of 1 m and 5 m—were compared with JPL Horizons. Each comparison contains 577 aligned observations. The maximum reported elevation difference was approximately 0.000024 degrees, while azimuth differences were at or below approximately 0.000001 degrees. This independently checks apparent ephemeris directions for the tested observer and interval; it does not validate terrain obstruction.

Benefits and Intended Impact

LUNAR makes environmental constraints and modelling assumptions easier to inspect during preliminary lunar mission planning. It helps users understand how terrain, observer height and changing celestial geometry affect local visibility. Rather than producing an opaque overall site score, it exposes the underlying terrain profiles, time-dependent calculations and coverage limitations.

Technology and Tools

The project uses Python, NumPy, Pandas, Rasterio, GDAL, PROJ, SpiceyPy, NAIF SPICE, Streamlit and Plotly. NASA LOLA elevation products and JPL Horizons provide the scientific data and independent ephemeris reference. The prototype is software-only and does not require specialised hardware.

Creativity and Design

Its central design approach combines multi-resolution lunar terrain with time-dependent apparent celestial disks in a single interactive environment. It also exposes observer-height sensitivity, terrain coverage and sampled scheduling comparisons rather than inventing uncomputed candidate sites or arbitrary rankings.

Factors Considered and Limitations

The current demonstration covers one provisional Site01 tile-centre test point, two observer heights, a 45 km range-limited terrain horizon and a 48-hour ephemeris interval. Terrain beyond 45 km may raise the true skyline. DEM uncertainty is not fully propagated, and local DEM slope is not applied to the surface normal. Earth visibility does not guarantee DSN connectivity, and Sun visibility does not predict electrical power. The prototype is intended for preliminary exploration, not landing-site certification or operational mission decisions.

AI/SI Acknowledgement: ChatGPT (OpenAI) assisted with architecture, substantial first-draft code and test scaffolding, debugging, technical review, data interpretation, documentation and presentation design. Claude (Anthropic) provided independent technical reviews, validation guidance and resource-use research. I reviewed and tested the implementation and made the final project decisions. NASA LOLA and NAIF SPICE inputs are original scientific resources; LUNAR's numerical outputs are generated through deterministic calculations, not directly by a generative AI model.
